title: Fill a Bag
passage:
By mid-afternoon the hall smells of other people’s wardrobes. The trestles down the long side are covered end to end, but the covering is low and even, the way a field is even after the pickers. A jacket that would have ___(1)___ two pounds at half past ten goes at three for whatever coin is held out. Whether the hall is worth ___(2)___ open for a last hour is not decided on the takings.

At four the prices come off. Nobody announces it. The saucers of coins go to one end of the trestle, nothing has a price after that, and the afternoon moves from a sale to a ___(3)___. About a dozen people are left. Two are looking. The rest have come to carry, and both sides know it. “Nobody’s buying after four,” says Irene Dunnicott, who has run the sale for fourteen years. “They’re doing us a favour, and I’d rather say so than pretend.”

The obvious reading of a picked-over table is that the village looked at these things and said no. The arrival times say otherwise. Boxes come in all day, and the ones that arrive after two are the ones their owners have been circling all week: the good coat, the tea set, the thing that was somebody’s. Those are on the trestles at five not because the village refused them but because they were ___(4)___ offered. What is left at that hour is sorted by arrival time at least as much as by taste.

The pattern is not a law, and Dunnicott names the exceptions before anybody asks: the bag of curtain hooks on the same trestle since ten, the coat that came in at four and went in eleven minutes. ___(5)___, she can walk the tables at five and say which hour a thing came in, and be wrong about one in four. What that means, if it means anything, is that the things a household finds hardest to give up are the ones most likely to be left. At ten past five a man carries a standard lamp out to a car on the grass, watched from the doorway by the woman who brought it in.
– Wendy Bowles

questions.rationale: The answer is D. The frame gives an object and a sum of money at a stated hour, which in English is the fixed use of fetch: a thing fetches a price when it is sold. The rest of the sentence, where the same jacket goes at three for whatever coin is held out, sets two prices for one object side by side, and only fetch takes an inanimate subject in that construction. A, earned, is the near miss a careless reader takes first, because earning money is what the whole afternoon is for; but a jacket does not earn, a person or a stall does. B, gained, is the same misfit one step further out: gain takes an abstract object such as ground, weight or an advantage, not a price at a sale. C, returned, borrows the vocabulary of an investment, where a sum is what a holding returns over time, and a garment on a trestle for one morning is not that. All four are ordinary past participles of verbs about getting money, so no option can be ruled out on register or on part of speech, and the discrimination is the collocation itself.

The answer is C. Worth in this use is followed by a gerund, and what is kept open is the hall, so worth keeping open is the only licensed form. A, keep, is the bare form and cannot follow worth at all. B, kept, puts a past participle after worth, and worth takes no past participle: worth kept open is no more English than worth said. D, to keep, is the commonest error in this frame and should collect most of the wrong answers, because worth is one of the few words in English that refuses the infinitive where near neighbours such as able or ready accept it. All four are forms of one ordinary verb, so the set is uniform in part of speech and nothing is ruled out by meaning; only the complement rule decides it.

The answer is B. The two clauses before the gap take the prices away altogether, and the sentence contrasts what the afternoon was, a sale, with what it becomes, so the word in the gap has to name an event at which nothing is charged. A, clearance, is the strongest distractor and dies on that contrast: a clearance is a kind of sale, with prices on the goods, so an afternoon cannot move from a sale to one. C, markdown, names a reduction in a price and so assumes the prices the passage has just said are gone; it also belongs to shop vocabulary rather than to a hall with saucers of coins on a trestle. D, liquidation, is the winding up of a company and its assets, so it fails on register and on sense at once. All four are nouns for a downward turn in price or trade, so none can be removed for being the wrong sort of word.

The answer is B. The sentence carries an explicit contrast – not because the village refused them but because – so what follows has to be a reason that is not refusal, and the paragraph has already named the quantity in question: time on the table. Of the two options at the small end of the scale only briefly combines with offered in that sense. C, thinly, is at the small end too, but it measures spread rather than duration, and goods on a trestle are not thinly offered. D, openly, is the mirror at the other end and is live English, which is what makes it dangerous; it is the choice of a reader who takes the sentence to mean that the coats were on show and passed over, but a thing passed over after being on show has been refused, which is the reading the sentence has just excluded. A, amply, is the second option at the large end and fails on the collocation as well as on the pole. Two options sit at each end of the scale and each end holds exactly one live combination with offered, so the pole removes two and the collocation removes two, and only the two together reach the answer.

The answer is A. The sentence before the gap gives away the exceptions, two of them, and the sentence after the gap returns to the claim and says how far it holds, so the connective has to mark a claim surviving a concession that has already been made. B, granted, is the near miss and the reason this gap is not easy: granted opens a concession, and the concession is in the previous sentence, so putting granted in front of the claim makes the claim the thing being conceded, which reverses the paragraph. C, therefore, reads the exceptions as grounds for the claim, but a list of counterexamples does not produce the generalisation they fail to fit. D, afterwards, marks the next thing in a sequence, and there is no sequence here: the sentence before the gap names two exceptions rather than an event that the walk down the tables could follow, and what comes after the gap is a standing claim about what she can do at five on any day and how often she is wrong. Each of the four is a connective, each opens an English sentence naturally and takes the comma and the full clause that follow, so the gap turns on the discourse relation and not on the class or the shape of the option.

G-STEM q:3 (register 2+2, low, blind pick A = a distractor): the split is giveaway (informal, extreme) and liquidation (a business being wound up) against the two neutral retail terms. No single substitution closes it. Replacing liquidation with another neutral retail noun (discount, reduction) makes two distractors die for identical reasons, which is a redundancy channel of its own; replacing one of the neutral pair with a marked term turns a 2+2 into a 3+1 that points a test-wise reader at a single distractor. The markedness axis IS the gap type here (register/sense), the heuristic points AWAY from the key, and G-DISTRACTOR passed the set with zero findings. Left as designed.

G-STEM q:4 (PAIR_STRUCTURE, low, blind pick C = a distractor): amply/thinly are contradictories on one variable. Closing this needs amply replaced, and every replacement examined either creates a second defensible answer in the frame (reluctantly, quietly, lately - each of which is a reason that is not refusal, which is exactly what the sentence asks for), reuses a barred string (widely, shipped in elf-b20-002), or deepens the retail cross-question register (cheaply). This set was already rebuilt once in drafting (more/less/longer/shorter was cut for two clean dyads). Left, deliberately, and flagged for V-FINAL rather than churned.
